newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Samsung mulls A$200 mln Australia facility.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Samsung mulls A$200 mln Australia facility.

text.p: South Korea's big Samsung and Co Ltd is considering establishing a A$200 million staff education and training centre on the east coast of Australia.

The plan, which would accompany a large-scale Australian investment programme in commodities, would be designed to train the group's more than 200,000 employees in Western culture as well as in company matters, Peter (J.G.) Park, managing director of Samsung (Australia) Pty Ltd, told Reuters.
A consensus was emerging on the plan to establish the centre in Australia, after "persistent persuasion", Park said.

The Samsung plan, which would follow Hong Kong-based Cathay Pacific's establishment of a A$250 million data centre in Australia last year on cost grounds, was partly based on property and general cost considerations, Park said.
Other attractions were the environment, transportation and telecommunications infrastructure, weather and frequency of flights between Australia and Korea.

Australia's location in the Asian time zone was also important. "Most importantly, jet lag of only one hour is almost negligible, even though it is (a) long distance (between Australia and Korea)," Park said.
Apart from costs, Australia's attraction for Samsung is its culture. "To globalise our concept, to be trained in Western culture might be beneficial, attractive, meaningful," Park said.
Samsung was also considering investing in Australian residential and commercial property, he said.
These and other planned moves by Samsung show an interest in Australia which extends beyond the established Australia-Japan connection of the raw materials trade.

Samsung has invested in Australian meat and is planning to become a major producer of wheat. But it is also negotiating with several Australian food manufacturers to export processed and packaged food products to South Korea, Park said.
Products included health food, dairy food products, canned foods and wines.
Next year the group expected to export about A$10 million worth of packaged and processed Australian food, he said.

With Samsung engaged in a US$3 billion programme to establish its own supermarket and department store chain in Korea, the group is emerging as a direct link between Australian food and Korean shoppers.
The supermarket link is part of the explanation for why Samsung sees profits in Australian beef while the Australian industry struggles with falling prices and demand.

Access to the Korean market would come not just through the gradual opening up of the country's import system, but through Samsung's plans to directly place upgraded and better-packaged Australian beef on its own supermarket shelves.

Samsung also would bring a "spirit of enterprise", holistic resources management, systematic data collection, genetic management and greater planning for pasture quality to its beef enterprises, Park said.
Now is a good time to buy depressed Australian rural properties, according to Park. It might even give "some small encouragement to Australian traditional farmers," he added.
